The sensitivity analyses are a very large amount of machinery for 45 cells. The 13 rule variants, the leave-one-source-out recounts, the status-flip search up to four flips and the 220 minimal sets produce counts of hypothetical recodings that are not tied to any evidence-based uncertainty. The paper also states that the weak-support scenario is chosen arbitrarily. These analyses do not strengthen the claims.

The D2 coding conflates what the model said with what it believed. It accepts post-hoc follow-up answers as documented, even though the sources themselves call them biased or elicited. Examples are Opus 4.6, AISI Mythos 5 (where the developer calls the answer 'essentially impossible') and Opus 4.7 (where the model ignored permission during the run). Under baseline D2 is 'documented' for five cells. This weakens RQ2, which the paper then says cannot be answered.

The rule S1 labelled 'strict D2: verbatim only' retains only Hugging Face D2. That cell was itself flipped by an AI re-check, and it points the opposite way (the agent knew the action was out of scope). The paper presents RQ2 as answered by a single cell that carries a contested coding history.

The numbers in the Hugging Face D1 conflict are not fully reconciled. Human answers Q4 (unknown) and Q5/Q6 (documented) conflict and were 'recorded through defaults rather than typed replies'. The paper switches the cell to documented and reports 39/6 as S5. Which reading is baseline is therefore a procedural accident that moves headline counts.

Many sources are not reauthenticated. R01 and R05 returned HTTP 403, and R11–R23 are not reauthenticated. R18's link was derived from the DOI and never opened. Several closest-work comparisons rely on a 'verified summary' (Steegen) or on abstracts only (Greenblatt, CaMeL). The Bouke concordance (11 rows, 4 matches) is not verified. The paper reports no agreement count, but the comparison with the closest work is thin.

The references and ledger are padded. The ledger holds 70 sources, yet R36–R70 support no coded proposition. The bibliography includes many unrelated items (GRADE, QCA, intelligence analysis, Zenodo and SSRN items, authorization papers) that are never cited in the text. The brief's 6-page limit is met only by moving most of the analysis into appendices (A–F), which is a format-workaround concern.

The quotation-presence and protocol checks verify only that quotes occur and that tables match the coded data. They do not test entailment. The 'PASS' therefore says nothing about whether the coded statuses are right, and the paper says so itself. Partial-support grading was not performed.
strengths: The paper is unusually candid about its limits. It states single coding, the AI revisions, the lack of an agreement coefficient and the absence of any prevalence or efficacy claim. It also disclaims novelty for each prior-work overlap.
Each coding decision retains a proposition, a quoted passage, a locator, references and qualifications. The data files make the 45-cell matrix traceable to the sources.

The paper separates reachability from permission, an attributed statement from actual authority, detection from containment, and attempt from effect. It also separates organization-level reporting from whole-proposition support and warns that organizational separation does not imply independent observation.

Reporting the rule variants side by side, with provenance of status changes, exposes how the results depend on the coding rules. Examples are the baseline versus S1 for D2, and the S6 provenance recount.
The study is documentary only, with no probing of real systems. Descriptions stay at the level of detail in the public sources.

strengths: The complete 45-cell table and supplied coded data provide unusually explicit propositions, source locators, quotations, qualifications and revision histories.
The study consistently distinguishes reachability from permission, attributed statements from stable belief, stopping from containment, and reported effects from downstream harm.
Dependent units, shared-source observations, purposive selection and the limits of organizational corroboration are acknowledged explicitly.
The alternative D2 and effect rules expose substantial interpretive sensitivity rather than concealing it behind a single aggregate result.
The topic is relevant to an agent-security workshop, and the manuscript appropriately avoids prevalence estimates and causal defense-efficacy claims.

reasons: The broad incident comparison, authorization distinction, reporting dimensions, and sensitivity methods strongly overlap with listed work and do not establish methodological novelty.

The concrete increment is a reproducible 45-cell evidence artifact linking support decisions to deciding passages, locators, source organisations, coding-change provenance, and rule-variant recounts. No listed description establishes this particular artifact or audit.

Separating organisation-level reporting from whole-proposition support adds a checkable corpus-specific analysis, provided organisation counts are not presented as independent corroboration or evidence quality.

The corrected claims acknowledge substantive sensitivity: only D2 having the most unknown cells survives all three stated coding variants; the two-organisation finding depends on the lead's reread. This supports a bounded audit contribution rather than a general security finding.
The contribution text is truncated, so this verdict applies to the explicit current claim supplied and does not certify the underlying artifacts or numerical accuracy.
novelty.reposition: Present the paper as a reproducible evidence-audit extension of existing incident comparisons, centered on passage-linked coding and provenance-separated recounts. Lead with the surviving D2 evidence gap, and report the organisational-support and D5 results explicitly as coding-dependent descriptions of this disclosure corpus.
